[20/12/2023, 09:38:27] 🤴🏽👑KingMichael👑🤴🏽: *_CLASSIFICATION OF PSYCHIATRIC DISORDERS_* 

Psychiatric disorders are classified using the _International classification of diseases, (ICD- 10)_, 10th Revision, 1992 also referred to as the WHOs classification for all diseases and the diagnostic and statistical manual of Mental Disorders, (DSM-IV-TR) IV Edition developed by the American Psychiatric Association (APA) for the classification of psychiatric disorders.
The chapter in ICD-10 where psychiatric disorders are classified is *F which classifies* psychiatric disorders as mental and behavioural disorders (MBDs)* and assigns codes on an alphanumeric system from F00 - F99 as follows;

*F00-F09: Organic cases, including symptomatic mental disorders*

This class is predisposed by demonstrable cerebral disease such as primary brain pathology or brain dysfunction due to systemic disease. E.g. dementia, organic amnesic syndrome and delirium 

*F10-F19: Behavioural and mental disorders secondary to psychoactive substance abuse*

Examples include drug abuse, amnesic syndrome, acute intoxication, and withdrawal state and dependence syndrome.


*F20-F29: Schizophrenia, schizotypal and delusional disorders*

Psychiatric disorders in this class are characterized by prominent disturbance of thought, perception, affect, and/or behaviour. E.g. schizophrenia, schizoaffective disorders, schizotypal disorder, induced delusional disorder and persistent delusional disorders. 

*F31-F39: Affective disorders i.e. mood disorders*
 
This class includes behavioural and mental disorders characterized by a significant disturbance of mood. Examples include bipolar affective disorder, manic episode, depressive episode, recurrent depressive disorder and persistent mood disorder. 

*F40-F48: Neurotic, stress-related and somatoform disorders*

Neurotic disorders are predisposed by psychological abnormalities, examples are; phobias, anxiety disorders, obsessive compulsive disorder, dissociative and adjustment disorders.

*F50-F59: Behavioural syndrome i.e.*
 psychosomatic disorders
These psychiatric disorders are associated with physical factors or physiological abnormalities, examples include; sleep and eating disorders, non-organic sexual dysfunction etc. 

*F60-F69: Disorders of adult behaviour and personality*

This class is characterised by a persistent abnormal social and family lifestyle. Examples include; gender identity disorder, behavioural disorder associated with development and orientation, specific personality disorders, habit and impulse disorders.

*F70-F79: Mental retardation*

Patients in this class present with incomplete mental development and lack of intellectual abilities which may be secondary to other physical or mental disorders.  

*F80-F89: Disorders of psychological development*

These psychiatric disorders e.g. developmental disorders of motor function begin at infancy or childhood resulting in a delay or impairment in the development of functions that are linked to biological maturation of the central nervous system.  Other examples are; specific disorders of speech and language, mixed specific developmental disorders, developmental disorders of scholastic skills and pervasive development disorders. 

*F90-F98: Behavioural and emotional disorders*

These psychiatric disorders also have an early onset in childhood or adolescence; examples are mixed disorders of emotions and conduct, hyperkinetic disorders etc

[29/12/2023, 09:18:57] Faith A Ypgd: To add to what has been said about this, a Full Time Pharmacist may be employed to assist the Superintendent Pharmacist, especially in big organisations where the duties of the Superintendent are overwhelming.

The Superintendent Pharmacist registers the Pharmacist, not the Full Time Pharmacist.

The Locum Pharmacist's employment is on a contract basis and may not be fully accountable to the organisation. But for a Full Time Pharmacist, he/she is on a full time employment with the organisation and fully accountable to them.

Some Organisations employ Full Time Pharmacist instead of contracting Locum Pharmacist to ensure a level of stability in work flow.

Hope this helps. ‎<This message was edited>

[02/01/2024, 21:03:22] ~ Baba Adugbo 🕵️‍♂️: PCN PROCEDURE FOR 2024 ANNUAL LICENCE RENEWAL.
Complement of the season Noble colleagues.
Procedures for licence renewal are as follows.
1. Click this link https://pay.pcn.gov.ng/Identity/Account/Login to registration as stakeholder. Use your registration number as activation code.

2. Once registered, login and select pharmacist activities, Annual License, appropriate year and appropriate years post graduation. 

3. Pay the appropriate amount for your annual License. 

4. Collect scratch from PCN office on Presentation of payment receipt and PSN clearance form to PCN office.

5. Login to pcncoreapp  https://www.pcn.gov.ng/online-registration/ to submit your 2024 license.

NOTE: If your registration number is not activated, fill the following information and send to PCN State officer.

i. Pharmacist registration number:

ii. Pharmacist Name:

iii. Phone number:

iv. Email address:

V. Year of full registration: 

vi. Area of practice:

vii. State of Practice:

Thank you.

‎[03/01/2024, 09:26:10] ~ Dr. Favvy☺️: Anaemia is a common blood disorder that occurs when the body has fewer red blood cells than normal.

It is often a symptom of a disease rather than a disease itself.  In some cases, it may be temporary and caused by a nutritional deficiency or blood loss but in other cases, it is as a result of a chronic or hereditary condition.

While many types of anaemia can be mild and easily corrected, certain other types can be severe, chronic, and/or life-threatening...

[03/01/2024, 22:35:27] PHARM(DR)OTAKHOR JENNIFER: Good afternoon Men of honour. 
Below information is

 *Step by Step guide to making payment on the PCN Payment Portal for Registered Stakeholders* (i.e. Pharmacists, Pharm Tech, PPMVL, Pharmacy Premises)

✅Access the portal by visiting www.pay.pcn.gov.ng
For the first time users,  

✅select the “Register Stakeholder”

✅Enter your Pharmacists or pharmacists Technician or PPMVL or Premises Registration Number

✅If you want your Registration number to remain as your username, you leave the username as it is, otherwise you could change it
Enter and confirm your password of your choice
Then submit.

✅ This will take you to login where you are expected login with your new username and password

✅Select the make payment option

✅Select generate new payment

✅Select payment category
Select current year

✅Select payment type

✅Select self for your payment otherwise select stakeholders for premises 

✅If the payment is for a premise, search with the three letters of the premises name

✅Select add to the category
After adding, you could still edit or remove payment if not sure

✅Select pay now

✅Enter the payment description

✅Select the mode of payment (either online or bank)

✅If bank or card, generate print your invoice and proceed to make payment

 Signed 
 *Pharm Yusuf Abdulmujib 
PCN Sokoto State officer*

*Congratulations to MEDVAX Health!*


The United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) is thrilled to announce the 14 Winners of the *4HerPower Challenge*, a collaborative initiative between UNFPA, Organon and MIT Solve, dedicated to enhancing sexual and reproductive health and rights (#SRHR) for and by youths. UNFPA made the announcement on Monday, 8 January, 2024.

CONGRATULATIONS to *Pharm (Dr) Chioma Uzoma* and *Pharm (Dr) Favour Ogedegbe* (both distinguished alumni of the Department of Pharmacy, University of Benin) of MEDVAX Health, as their *Medtracka App* was among the 14 Winners (the only Winner from Nigeria)!

MEDVAX made it to the top 20, out of about 400 contestants. All winners will share a huge amount of funding, and would embark on a 6-month support programme, to fuel their innovations for meaningful, equitable, and sustainable SRHR advancements.

MEDVAX Health will be working with the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) and UNFPA for the next 6 months, to launch the *Medtracka App*.

You would recall that on 26 September 2023, MEDVAX Health emerged as the runner-up in the *Bechangemaker* competition organized by WorldSkills and HP Foundation, at Dublin, Ireland.

Congratulations, MEDVAX Health!

*MEMBER SPOTLIGHT: Pharm (Dr.) Onyeka Favour Onwughai*


Pharm (Dr.) Onyeka Favour Onwughai, an alumni of the Department of Pharmacy, University of Benin (UNIBEN), is a Data Scientist with deep interest in machine learning and Artificial Intelligence (AI).


Dr. Onyeka is a Startup founder, the Team Lead at "finds my meds". Find my meds (findmymeds.com) is a web app that is set to be launched this January 2024. Find my meds aims to solve the challenges of out of stock (o/s). A Pharmacist can easily search for a medication that is rare or o/s through the platform, for a patient who needs the meds. The platform will give a list of the closest Pharmacies to one's location that has the o/s med(s) and one can go on to contact them and procure for the patient. Find my med creates a scenario that no matter the drug that is being searched for, a Pharmacist will never have to tell the patient that it is not available. The patient can be required to wait for about 10–15 minutes, while the Pharmacist finds the med(s).

Dr. Onyeka is also the Chief Information Officer (CIO) at Rxpressdrug Pharma, where he (and the CTO) is in charge of all technical stuffs such as coding, building the websites and apps and fixing technical issues. He's also the Head at PIT Innovation labs (PIT Africa).


Dr. Onyeka Onwughai was present at the Tech fest event (as a panelist) during the Young Pharmacists Group (YPG) 4th Annual National Conference in Rivers State (2023).

He also emerged the winner of the Scholar Nature Data Science and machine learning bootcamp 2020, a bootcamp which had over 170 participants from 5 African countries.

Dr. Onyeka Onwughai has spoken to hundreds of youth across Africa on the subject of applying technology to healthcare and he's always looking for ways to merge Technology and Health.


Dr Onyeka shared about his journey in Tech so far..

Dr Onyeka: My journey into tech has been a bittersweet experience. It has been filled with mixed emotions. It could be because I'm not just into it for the money, but mainly due to my interest in solving problems and contributing to the society in my own little way and this comes with it's own challenges. One thing I've noticed in Nigeria is how people in authority most times resist change, even when they've been shown clearly how the change will benefit everyone in the long run. On one hand, I'm happy that I'm able to actually contribute to the betterment of our healthcare system, but on the other hand there is systemic resistance to change, which is sort of a norm in Nigeria and this discourages a lot of young people from even trying. But this has not discouraged me. One of my forte is being persistent once I'm convinced about something.

Dr Onyeka also shared how YPs who are interested in tech, could get into tech, the pros and cons.

Dr Onyeka: Tech is now much easier to learn than ever. This is because we are in the information age and just a little google search will give you more than enough materials you need to actually learn if one is serious. The first step, I believe, is getting a general knowledge of the different areas in tech so one can choose to specialize in the one that fascinates the person the most. One could do that by getting a mentor to walk the person through, in case one doesn't have. I can always be contacted, if one wants to be linked up with someone in his/her field of interest. Another thing I would say is that one shouldn't do tech just for the money. Although money is not a bad motivation, the problem is that many people see it as a get-rich-quick scheme. When these people don't get the money on time based on the deadline they set for themselves, they begin to get frustrated. This happens a lot.

In Nigeria, we need more Creators and Innovators. I am a Creator. People who will learn tech to actually solve the problems that we face daily as Nigerians, especially in the healthcare profession. Although starting up something from the ground comes with lots of challenges, but in the long run, if you're able to surmount those challenges, you will have created a fortune for yourself, inspired more people to solve more problems and also made the entrepreneurial environment less harsher for newbies. Just like it is in the west, the big companies and founders really play a major role in the success of small startups.


We are proud of what Pharm (Dr.) Onyeka F. Onwughai has been doing in the Tech and Health World. These contributions will keep making the Health World better, and impacting lives of many positively.

You can reach Dr. Onyeka F. Onwughai on +2348181243806

[15/01/2024, 11:18:53] Dr. Joshua Idemudia (PharmD) Ypgd: PCN PROCEDURE FOR 2024 ANNUAL LICENCE RENEWAL.
Complement of the season Noble colleagues.
Procedures for licence renewal are as follows.
1. Click this link https://pay.pcn.gov.ng/Identity/Account/Login to registration as stakeholder. Use your registration number as activation code.

2. Once registered, login and select pharmacist activities, Annual License, appropriate year and appropriate years post graduation. 

3. Pay the appropriate amount for your annual License. 

4. Collect scratch from PCN office on Presentation of payment receipt and PSN clearance form to PCN office.

5. Login to pcncoreapp  https://www.pcn.gov.ng/online-registration/ to submit your 2024 license.

NOTE: If your registration number is not activated, fill the following information and send to PCN State officer.

i. Pharmacist registration number:

ii. Pharmacist Name:

iii. Phone number:

iv. Email address:

V. Year of full registration: 

vi. Area of practice:

vii. State of Practice:

*PAGET'S DISEASE*


Annually, *January 11*, is the International Paget's Awareness Day. It's an opportunity to create awareness about PAGET'S Disease of the Bone.

Paget's Disease of the bone (osteitis deformans) is a disease that disrupts the replacement of old bone tissue with new bone tissue. Paget's disease of bone most commonly occurs in the pelvis, skull, spine and legs. Risk factors include increasing age and a family history of the condition. Over time, affected bones may become fragile and misshapen.

This condition can be symptomless for a long period of time. When symptoms do occur, they may include bone deformities, broken bones and pain in the affected area. Pain can occur: in the back, bones, hip, joints, or neck. Also common is: bone deformities, bone fracture, bowleggedness, gait abnormality, headache, joint stiffness, or pins and needles.

Medications for Paget's Disease of the bone include osteoporosis drugs (bisphosphonates), which are the most common treatment. Bisphosphonates are typically given by injection into a vein, but they can also be taken by mouth.

There are other types of PAGET'S Disease. We have:
Paget's disease of the nipple or breast – a rare type of breast cancer.
Paget's disease of the penis – a rare type of penile cancer.
Paget's disease of the vulva – a rare type of vulval cancer.

*DID YOU KNOW?*

ACUTE DECOMPENSATED HEART FAILURE (ADHF)


*ADHF* can be defined as the sudden or gradual onset of the signs or symptoms of heart failure (dyspnea, swelling in the lower limbs, fatigue, etcetera) requiring unplanned office visits, emergency room visits, or hospitalization.

When heart failure becomes severe enough to cause symptoms requiring immediate medical treatment, it is called *decompensated heart failure (DHF)*. On the other hand, if one have heart failure but the heart is still functioning well enough that one don't have symptoms or have stable symptoms, the person have *compensated heart failure*.

The most common causes of acute decompensated heart failure are medication and dietary noncompliance. However, acute coronary syndrome, arrhythmias, uncontrolled hypertension, and infections such as endocarditis may also cause ADHF.

*NEGLECTED TROPICAL DISEASES (NTDs)*


*Neglected Tropical Diseases (NTDs)* are a diverse group of conditions that are mainly prevalent in tropical areas, where they thrive among people living in impoverished communities. They are caused by a variety of pathogens such as viruses, bacteria, parasites, fungi and toxins. NTDs can result to devastating health, negative social and economic consequences.

World NTDs Day is marked annually on January 30. This date marks the launch of the first WHO road map and the launch of the London declaration on neglected tropical diseases (NTDs), both in 2012.

There are several NTDs. They include: Buruli ulcer; Chagas disease; dengue and chikungunya; dracunculiasis; echinococcosis; foodborne trematodiases; human African trypanosomiasis; leishmaniasis; leprosy; lymphatic filariasis; mycetoma, chromoblastomycosis and other deep mycoses; noma; onchocerciasis; rabies; scabies and other ectoparasitoses; schistosomiasis; soil-transmitted helminthiases; snakebite envenoming; taeniasis/cysticercosis; trachoma; and yaws.

[18/01/2024, 16:05:16] David Ypg Edo PRO: STILL ON *DID YOU KNOW SERIES💥*

On Friday, 15 December 2023, WHO officially announced *Noma (cancrum oris or gangrenous stomatitis)* as a Neglected Tropical Disease. The WHO in a statement noted that the decision which was recommended by the 17th meeting of the Strategic and Technical Advisory Group for Neglected Tropical Diseases underscores its commitment to expanding health services to the world’s most vulnerable populations.

*Noma* is a severe gangrenous disease of the mouth and face, that primarily affects malnourished young children (between the ages of two and six) in regions of extreme poverty. It starts as an inflammation of the gums, which, if not treated early, spreads quickly to destroy facial tissues and bones. It frequently leads to death, with survivors suffering severe disfigurement.

Evidence indicates that Noma is caused by bacteria found in the mouth. There are multiple risk factors associated with this disease, including poor oral hygiene, malnutrition, weakened immune systems, infections, and extreme poverty. Noma isn’t contagious but tends to strike when the body’s defenses are down.

Early detection is essential, as therapy is most effective at the early stages of the disease when it causes severe swollen gums, known as acute necrotizing gingivitis. Treatment involves antibiotics, advice, and support on practices to improve oral hygiene with disinfectant mouthwash (salt water or chlorhexidine could be used) and nutritional supplements.

If diagnosed during the early stages of the disease, treatment can lead to proper wound healing without long-term consequences. In severe cases though, surgery may be necessary. Children who survive the gangrenous stage of the disease are likely to suffer severe facial disfigurement, have difficulty eating and speaking, face social stigma and isolation, and need reconstructive surgery.

Noma is often managed by oral health programmes in endemic areas and collaboration with NTD programmes at the operational level can be strengthened, notably by integrating noma within the activities aimed at detecting and managing skin-related neglected tropical diseases (skin NTDs).

A new species of mosquito is driving up malaria infections in Africa, fuelling a growing public health concern.

The _Anopheles stephensi_ mosquito, shortened by some entomologists to "steve", has so far been detected in seven African countries, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).

The mosquito, which originated in South Asia, was first detected in Djibouti in 2012. Since then, malaria rates in the country have grown exponentially.

The new species has since spread to Ethiopia, Kenya, Nigeria and Ghana.

Unlike other mosquitoes that breed in rivers and swamps, “steve” is known to be an urban breeder that thrives in dry areas.

It only needs a bit of moisture, like water trapped in containers, tyres and gutters to survive.

The species also bites outdoors during the day and is immune to commonly used pesticides.

“It’s a threat in urban settings, it’s a threat to our strategies in place now because we’re mostly using indoor strategies. It’s also difficult to detect and is very resistant. It stays in very harsh climates and is very difficult to eliminate from an environment,” Dr Dorothy Achu, the WHO lead for tropical diseases in Africa, says.

[19/01/2024, 23:17:12] Mr Michael Ypg State Cordinator: Teamwork, Rivalry Between Nigerian Professionals, and My Experience in Academia

19.01.2024

I reported to the Department of Electric Power Engineering for my postdoc on the 1st of October 2013. After the reception, I was taken to the office I will be using for the 2 years I will spend in Norway. It has a brand-new Dell laptop and a Dock to connect to a monitor supplied with it. Before I can step into the lab, I must do a safety course. One is an online test which I have to pass before the physical safety lecture with the head of technical staff. They got my foot size and ordered a brand-new safety boot. The rule is that I can't step into the lab or workshop without the boot. Safety first. 

A few days later, I was taken to the lab. And Lars Lundgaard, my supervisor, said, Abdel, this is where you will spend your 2 years. We all laughed. So, I began to set up the lab. After a few weeks on it and I thought I was done, I called my Professor to have a look. He checked all the connections and he said the setup was ok. I was happy and looking forward to switching it on. My thought was that his "ok" was all I needed to start work but he said there was one more step to cross before I could turn the setup on. 
 
He said a designated senior technical staff needs to check that the experiment is well set up, all safety requirements satisfied, and safe for me to use. It's high voltage and you can't make any mistakes. The technical staff will then sign an approval form in which a copy is hung on the setup.

The senior technical staff in the department at NTNU was out of the office and he contacted an authorised technical staff from SINTEF who came for the assessment. He made some observations on the grounding of a part and asked me to correct it. My Professor told him that he would ensure I get that done and so he signed the form.

The process pushed me into deep thinking about our system in Nigeria. While most of us, including their just employed academics, are Mr. Know-it-All in our system and think we can run a lab without technical staff, a technical staff needs to assess and approve a setup in a Norwegian University lab before a researcher and research students can use it. Not a professor can bypass that process. The assessment is in the interest of the user, the facilities, and the research output. I experienced strong teamwork. 

There is a trending memo on a directive from NMA that reminds me of this internal rivalry among professionals within the Nigerian systems that is dragging us back. The politics among the academics. The rivalry between the academics and non-academics. The Abuja civil servants' hatred for university lecturers, especially if they happen to be in charge of a button to press against the academics.The rivalry between medical doctors and other health workers. 

We have the artificial barrier between engineering and physical sciences in the universities. You can't lecture engineering students if you don't have an engineering degree and COREN-registered Engineer. The mounted artificial barrier between medical and life sciences. Medical students were taught biochemistry by the biochemists in Life science for years. They ain't qualified to teach medical students any longer. Medical students must be taught by only lecturers with a medical degree. etc.  

The NMA directive was that the medical and dental practitioners engaged in teaching pharmacy students on clinical rotation/clerkship should discontinue such engagement with immediate effect. I saw the memo as another internal wrangling that I thought could have been sorted without affecting the system. The memo generated an interesting discussion on my Facebook wall. So I decided to read a bit about clinical clerkship and clinical pharmacy.

The narrow knowledge I got was that Clinical Pharmacists played an important role in ensuring that the medicines prescribed to patients are suitable. Clinical rotation/Clerkship is a medical term used in medical education to describe training to provide students with a practical and stimulating learning experience. The clinical students are allowed to participate in ward rounds along with the healthcare team and provide a wide variety of clinical services. Clinical rotation/Clerkship for pharmacy students is a similar practical training to improve the quality of clinical pharmacy. It is designed to provide the opportunity for the student to have direct patient contact, apply knowledge in real-time, and other associated pharmacy experiences.

Universities around the world do this as a collaboration between the College of Medicine and the School of Pharmacy. During ward visits, pharmacists assessed drug charts to ensure that prescriptions were safe, effective, economical, etc. The inclusion of clinical pharmacists in ward rounds was reported to have had a tremendous impact on the healthcare delivery system. It can reduce adverse drug events, improve communication, and enable collaborative decision-making.

The few hours of reading have just improved my knowledge of the role of clinical pharmacy in quality healthcare delivery. I saw one similarity in the role that the technical staff was mandated to play to ensure that I had safe lab work during my postdoctoral research work; the role of the Clinical Pharmacist to ensure that the medicines prescribed to patients were suitable. The role was for my safety, the safety of the equipment, and the anticipated result. A THIRD EYE SUPPORTING partner that I can't FORGET or IGNORE in my career.

When we have different professionals in a system, every professional has a clear role to play in making that system work. So why the rivalry among us instead of healthy competition to bring benefits to the system? Why can't we sit down to discuss our differences and come to an understanding? Why the mounted artificial barriers? What are we protecting? What role are professional bodies and Associations playing in bridging this gap? Or are they widening the gap?

I got a PhD from an Engineering Department where the 3 professors in the department who supervised me got their PhD in Engineering, Physics, and Chemistry. I always consider myself lucky to have worked with these great minds that injected different flavours (engineering, physics, and chemistry) into my PhD work and experience. Why can't we copy this? We have societies like IEEE, the largest engineering institution, that admit relevant members without barriers. Why ain't we copying this? We have some Nigerian professors in the US who are beneficiaries of the world of academics without borders but encouraging the barriers in the Nigerian system. 

We need to sit down to reflect on the gains of these ridiculous rivalries within our systems. We need to ask ourselves with all honesty if the so-called gains from the barriers are personal gains or a gain for the system. Let's reflect on the power of teamwork and collaborative decision-making. We need to put an end to these unnecessary rivalries and begin to dismantle these artificial barriers for effective teamwork toward repositioning our system, especially the university system.

Dear colleagues, despite the low pay,  people think you are earning more than your salary because they truly feel your value is that high. These people are looking up to us, academics, as the torch bearer of the nation. You are their brainbox. We must be seen playing that role instead of all these in-house fighting.

We can do it. We can work together to make our system work. We can make Nigeria great. We just need to keep our ego and selfish interests aside and work for the system.

©️Amoka

[20/01/2024, 09:50:13] Sir Hope Onyemaechi: ‼️‼️‼️PHARMACY COUNCIL OF NIGERIA HAS CHANGED ITS PAYMENT PORTAL
BELOW IS THE PROCEDURE FOR PAYMENT ON THE NEW PCN PAY PORTAL

*i. Guideline for Creating an Account as a Stakeholder (Licensed Pharmacist).*
a. Access the portal by visiting https://pay.pcn.gov.ng/Identity/Account/Register?returnUrl=%2F
b. Enter your PCN full registration number
c. Your details would pop up after some seconds to a minute
d. Enter and confirm a password of your choice
e. Login with your new login details (username: pharmacist full registration number and your new password)

*ii. Guide to Making Payments on the New PCN Pay Portal*
a. Visit https://pay.pcn.gov.ng/ and login with the details generated in (i) above.
b. Click on Make Payment
c. Click on Generate New Payment
d. Select the Appropriate Payment Category
e. Select Revenue and Payment years
f. Select the Appropriate Payment Type. (The amount to be paid will automatically display; however, in cases where the amount does not automatically display, please get in touch with the PCN office for clarification.)
g. If you are making a single payment, you can click on “Pay Now” at this point, but if you are making multiple payments, you should click on “Add to Payment Cart” till you have selected all the payments you are making before clicking “Pay Now.”
h. Select “Online Payment” as the preferred payment method.
i. Click on the “Remita” icon
j. At this point, you can make payment online using your ATM Card via the “Card Option” or obtain the RRR Code to take to the bank via the “Bank Branch” option.

*iii. General Payment Option for Non-Stakeholders and Those Without Accounts.*
a. Visit https://pay.pcn.gov.ng/
b. Click on “Make General Payment”
c. Select the appropriate Payment Category
d. Select the appropriate Payment Type. (The amount to be paid will automatically display; however, in cases where the amount does not automatically display, please get in touch with the PCN office for clarification.)
e. Enter the appropriate Payment Description
f. Select the appropriate State Location
g. Select Payer’s Name, Phone, and Email
h. Click on “Pay Now.”
i. Select “Online Payment” as the preferred payment method.
j. Click on the “Remita” icon
k. At this point, you can make payment online using your ATM Card via the “Card Option” or obtain the RRR Code to take to the bank via the “Bank Branch” option.

A new species of mosquito is driving up malaria infections in Africa, fuelling a growing public health concern.

The _Anopheles stephensi_ mosquito, shortened by some entomologists to "steve", has so far been detected in seven African countries, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).

The mosquito, which originated in South Asia, was first detected in Djibouti in 2012. Since then, malaria rates in the country have grown exponentially.

The new species has since spread to Ethiopia, Kenya, Nigeria and Ghana.

Unlike other mosquitoes that breed in rivers and swamps, “steve” is known to be an urban breeder that thrives in dry areas.

It only needs a bit of moisture, like water trapped in containers, tyres and gutters to survive.

The species also bites outdoors during the day and is immune to commonly used pesticides.

“It’s a threat in urban settings, it’s a threat to our strategies in place now because we’re mostly using indoor strategies. It’s also difficult to detect and is very resistant. It stays in very harsh climates and is very difficult to eliminate from an environment,” Dr Dorothy Achu, the WHO lead for tropical diseases in Africa, says.

[22/01/2024, 20:48:30] King Penet: 60 Herbs & Their Uses

Agnus Castus
Helps regulate progesterone levels in women, easing menopausal symptoms plus some menstrual problems such as breast tenderness and menstrually-related migraines and acne. Do not use if taking HRT. Can be combined with Black Cohosh, Sage and Feverfew as appropriate.

Aloe Vera
Aloe gel is a wonderful skin treatment. Can be used on burns, scars, wounds, acne, sunburn, varicose veins and ulcerated skin. Internally, can ease gastritis, peptic ulcers and irritable bowel syndrome.

Arnica
Arnica cream helps with bruising. Can also restore hair loss. Do not use the cream on broken skin, do not take arnica internally (except in tiny homeopathic doses), and never use undiluted arnica as it can be toxic.

Anise
Decoction of seeds with honey to relieve a cough.

Basil
Infusion to drink for migraines. Douche with it for yeast infection. Pregnant women should not have any basil.

Black Cohosh
Regulates estrogen production in women, helping with menstrual problems such as cramps, and useful during the menopause for reducing hot flashes and menopausal depression. Also helps with rheumatoid arthritis, some types of headache, osteoporosis, high blood pressure and tinnitus.

Borage
Stimulates the adrenal glands, useful in dangerous or stressful situations and for anxiety, depression and grief, giving us the courage to go on. Also helps with rheumatoid arthritis and acts as a diuretic and cleanser of the kidneys.

Buchu Leaf
Works as an antiseptic in the urinary system, relieving cystitis, thrush, prostate problems and all urinary tract diseases. Also reduces catarrh and intestinal wind and bloating.

Caraway
Regulates menstruation and helps with cramps.

Cayenne
Relieves arthritis pain. Helps regulate blood sugar.

Celery
Sedative. Relieves hypertension. Helps the kidneys to detoxify the body.

Celery Seed
Eases arthritis pain, including osteoarthritis, and relieves gout with regular use. Helps with urinary tract infections such as cystitis. Can also ease chest problems such as asthma and bronchitis.

Chamomile Flowers
Mild sedative, helping with sleep problems. It also has anti inflammatory properties and is very useful for digestive problems including gastro-intestinal irritation, ulcers, colitis and irritable bowel. It can relieve cramps either related to indigestion or menstrual cramps. It also makes the body more receptive to other remedies, working well in combination.

Chickweed
It may come as a surprise to many gardeners to hear that this well-known and rampant weed has some good qualities! Chickweed cream can be very effective for eczema and other dry, irritated skin, as well as minor burns, stings and scars. It also helps relieve rheumatism.

Chicory
Dissolves gallstones. Cleans the liver.

Cilantro
Antibacterial. Relieves stomach upsets of bacterial origin. Helps to preserve meat.

Cinnamon
Helpful for bronchitis. For persistent coughs, use 4 drops of the essential oil in a bowl of boiling water and inhale the steam.

Clove
Clove oil is a wonderful remedy for toothache. Cloves also help against alcoholism.

Comfrey
This herb contains allantoin, which aids growth and healing in cartilage, bone and muscle. It has been used to help heal fractures and sprains for centuries. Reduces swelling. For external use only – apply as a poultice. Comfrey can also help with acne and scars – mix a teaspoonful of powdered comfrey root with water to make a paste and apply it as a face pack, leaving on for as long as possible.

Cramp Bark
Useful for any kind of cramps. In the case of menstrual cramps, start taking it a few days before menstruation is due. Also helps with menopausal aches and pains. Can also be used to help control the bladder in cases of incontinence or bedwetting, and for irritable bowel syndrome.

Damiana
This Mexican herb was prized as an aphrodisiac and traditionally is mainly used for male sexual problems including impotence and premature ejaculation. It can also be helpful in stimulating the reproductive organs in women and relieving menstrual pains. Also used for depression linked to nervous exhaustion, and urinary infections.

Dandelion
Dandelion leaves are used in salad in many countries. It is a great detoxifier, helping the liver, kidneys and gallbladder to eliminate waste. For warts, rub the wart with the white juice from a dandelion leaf or stem twice a day for a few weeks.

Devil’s Claw
Eases the pain of arthritis and rheumatism, and persistent back pain. Works as an anti-inflammatory, also useful for fevers. Stimulates the digestion.

Dill
Insomnia.

Echinacea Root
Boosts the immune system, with anti-viral and anti-bacterial effects. Good for flu, colds, throat infections, tonsillitis, and even ME (myalgic encephalomyelitis). Also for boils, tooth abscess and acne where body toxicity is the cause.

Fennel
Bad breath.

Fenugreek
Soothing for the digestive system, relieving problems such as colitis, ulcers, irritable bowel, gastro-enteritis and diarrhea. Fenugreek also has a reputation as an aphrodisiac and the seeds are used for male impotence in China.

Feverfew
Anti-inflammatory. Take small doses as a preventive treatment for migraine, especially menstruation-related migraines. Also effective for minor headaches, hangovers, and arthritic and rheumatic pain.

Garlic
Antibiotic, especially effective for bronchitis and other chest infections. Reduces blood cholesterol levels, reducing the risk of heart attacks. Thins the blood, helping to prevent strokes. Antiseptic and antifungal, helpful for athlete’s foot, infectious rashes and warts. Contraindications: may irritate the digestive tract in some people; not to be taken by nursing mothers as it can cause colic in the baby.

Ginger
Calms the gastro-intestinal tract, preventing travel sickness and nausea. May be useful for morning sickness in pregnancy (check with your doctor). Eases symptoms of colds, flu, bronchitis and whooping cough. Also thins the blood to reduce stroke risk.

Gingko Leaf
Aids memory and concentration by helping circulation in the brain, particularly for seniors. Is used to treat dementia. Antidepressant, helps to prevent strokes and thrombus, and relieves tinnitus. Taken by many multiple sclerosis sufferers.

Ginseng (Korean)
Relieves stress. Although generally a stimulant (including reputed aphrodisiac qualities for men) it will not prevent sleep if the body needs it. Improves health and spirits generally, especially in old age. Do not take with caffeine or alcohol, and do not use if you have hypertension. Siberian Ginseng is a milder form, but still should not be taken in these circumstances.

Golden Seal
Helpful for any problems with mucous membranes including respiratory ailments. Eases thrush in women, and athlete’s foot. Helps with peptic ulcers, liver problems and urinary infections, and stimulates the appetite.

Hawthorn Berry
Used under medical supervision for coronary heart disease and angina. Regulates blood pressure and helps stabilize irregular heartbeat. Not to be taken without medical advice.

Horseradish
Eases chest congestion. Relieves muscular aches.

Hyssop
Anti-inflammatory, widely used by asthma sufferers. Also helpful for hay fever and for colds (at the early stages). Relieves the nerves, preventing nervous diarrhea, and helps with nervous exhaustion, anxiety, depression, grief and guilt.

Lavender
Lavender oil can help relieve chilblains. Add a pinch of lavender flower to other mild herbal teas as a tonic, and to lime flower tea for migraine.

Lemon Balm (Melissa)
Calming and cheering, lemon balm can relieve mild depression, irritability, anxiety and panic. Can calm palpitations. Good for digestive problems caused by stress or anxiety. Externally, helps with herpes sores including cold sores.

Licorice
Balances the nervous system. Not to be used long term as it can damage the liver.

Lime Flower
For restlessness and nausea. Also helps with insomnia and migraine.

Marigold (Calendula)
Relieves skin problems including acne, rashes, cuts and sunburn. Essential oil can help relieve cold sores. Also helps with fungal infections including athlete’s foot, thrush and ringworm. Can be used for liver problems, including hepatitis.

Milk Thistle
For liver disorders, including all types of hepatitis, problems resulting from alcohol abuse, or to assist and protect the liver during chemotherapy (as always, discuss with your doctor). Also useful against melancholic depression which is associated with the liver.

Mint
There are many different species of mint. Garden mint tends to be milder than peppermint in its effects. Relieves heartburn and flatulence, helps stomach aches, nausea and travel sickness. Useful for head colds and flu, sore throats, headaches and eye infections. Antibacterial. Can help to lower a high temperature by provoking sweating.

Mustard
Relieves some types of heartburn. Helps with muscle sprains.

Nutmeg
Helps with indigestion.

Oregano
Reduces fever. Relieves indigestion, flatulence and bloating. Helps to regulate menstruation.

Parsley
High in vitamin C, but only if eaten raw. Also aids digestion, acts as a decongestant and diuretic, helps with bad breath, and cleans the blood.

Passiflora
A natural, non-addictive tranquilizer for anxiety, irritability, insomnia, excitability and panic. Antispasmodic, sometimes prescribed for convulsions, useful for hypertension, menstrual cramps and asthma.

Raspberry Leaf
High in calcium, useful for preventing osteoporosis. Heals wounds, relieves sore throats, canker sores and gingivitis (gum disease). For women, can control heavy menstrual bleeding and traditionally used in pregnancy to prevent nausea and miscarriage and relax the cervix in preparation for childbirth (as always, discuss with your doctor). Also good for post-natal depression.

Red Clover
Relieves eczema and psoriasis. Used in treatment of some cancers.

Rosemary
Stimulant for the heart and nervous system. Improves blood circulation to the brain and scalp, helping with migraines, hair loss, and to improve memory, especially for examinations. Helps with convalescence after a serious illness and increases optimism.

Sage
For all throat and gum infections. Also for menopausal hot flashes. Helps with irritable bowel and diarrhea. Relieves insect bites and stings. Is said to help with failing memory in old age. A versatile herb!

Slippery Elm
Good for digestive problems and disorders of the colon including constipation, colitis and hemorrhoids. Also for chest infections – colds, flu, bronchitis, pleurisy and even tuberculosis. Not to be taken in pregnancy.

St John’s Wort
Well known as an antidepressant. Also antiviral, used to treat flu, hepatitis and HIV. Can have side effects – only to be taken under medical supervision.

Tarragon
Helps with insomnia and depression.

Tea Tree
Tea tree oil is extracted from the leaves of a plant native to Australia. It has wonderful antiseptic powers and is also antifungal and rejuvenating. Helps with all surface problems of the body whether internal or external – problems of the skin including acne, mouth, sinus, bronchial passages, plus ear infections and dandruff.

Thyme
Antibiotic. Helps with asthma and respiratory tract infections.

Tumeric
Antioxidant.

Valerian
Tranquilizer and sleep remedy. Helpful in panic attacks. However, can have the side effect of causing headaches in some people.

Vervain
Relieves depression, especially after a viral illness like flu.

Willow Bark
The active ingredient in willow bark was extracted in the 19th century and found to be a very effective pain reliever. It is now produced synthetically as aspirin. Willow bark has the pain relieving and anti-inflammatory properties of aspirin, but does not thin the blood. Good for relieving arthritic pain.

Witch Hazel
Astringent, for external use on skin wounds, bruises and sprains. Helps rejuvenate sagging skin.

Yarrow
Aids blood clotting, helpful for wounds and nose bleeds. Used for some cardio-vascular conditions under medical supervision. Relieves catarrh and other symptoms of colds and flu.

Credits to Dr. Livy of TCAMPAN

[23/01/2024, 09:59:31] David Ypg Edo PRO: ⚠ Long Read⚠ 
*EASY WAYS TO PAY PCN FEES VIA THE PAY PORTAL WITHOUT GETTING DEBITED WITH NO RESULT*

Are you experiencing difficulties paying for your licenses via the PCN pay portal? 
Maybe you pay and you are debited and you don't get receipt even multiple times? Or you can't register on the portal at all? 
Don't worry, let Ifecita guide you with "love 😍 and belongingness"

💧 Most important thing to do is to create your profile by *registering as a stakeholder*. Paying with your profile will guarantee that you will get your *payment receipt once debited even if you got the notification that transaction failed*. 

💧To register as a stakeholder:
Visit pay.pcn.gov.ng
Click on *Register as a stakeholder*
Your activation code is *Your license number*
Other personal details would populate automatically. 
*Your user name is automated as your LICENSE NUMBER* which you can change to your email address if you want.
❤️ *VERY IMPORTANTLY, YOUR PASSWORD MUST HAVE A UPPERCASE/CAPITAL LETTER AND MUST BE ATLEAST 8 CHARACTERS* ❤️. You can save your new profile to your Google account for ease of access subsequently.

💧 Log in to your new profile.

💧 Click on *make payment*

💧 Select *Generate new payment*

💧 For *Payment Category* if you are paying for your personal license, *Select PHARMACISTS ACTIVITIES* and if it is Premises license *SELECT the category of premises you are registering* which could be RETAIL, WHOLESALE/DISTRIBUTION, IMPORTATION etc

💧 Upon selection of payment category, *Select Revenue Year*

💧 Select *Payment type* as applicable to you. The amount will automatically populate.

💧 *Do not edit the State location or Payee name*

💧 Click on *Add to payment cart*

💧 Then click on *Pay now* and respond to the prompt appropriately.

💧 Put in the Payment description as required which you could say *Personal license for Ifecita Gemma 2024* or *Premises license for "No Gree for Anybody Pharmacy" 2024* ☺

💧 Select *Mode of payment* as *Online*

💧 Click on the *Remitta logo that shows*

💧 *PLEASE PAY WITH YOUR A BANK CARD* and very importantly *copy out or screen grab your remitta number*

💧 ANOTHER important point to note *stay on the payment page until you are done and you get the notification of transaction successful from remitta*. Do not refresh until you are done and notified that payment is successful. You will be redirected to the PCN pay portal. 

💧When you are back to the payportal, you may get notification that *Payment unsuccessful or Payment successfully*
Whichever one, refresh the page. (you will likely be notified that duplicate payment) just click on cancel.

💧 Upon refreshing the payment portal, The tab that will open is *payment list*. So Select 
*invoice list as* PAID INVOICES
*Year generated*
And
*Month generated*

💧 Then click on *Fetch record* and voilà! You will see you payment history.

💧 Select the action *which is Print invoice*

You are now Done and dusted.

❤️SPECIAL ADVICE❤️
Kindly pay for everything one at a time please.
*most times merging invoices to pay doesn't go through* so patiently do them one by one. 

If you have any more challenge, you can reach out via WhatsApp 08165887040 (Service Charge May apply 😉) 🤗 

Sending you

*THE WORLD'S FIRST ROUTINE VACCINE PROGRAMME AGAINST MALARIA STARTS IN CAMEROON*


The world's first routine vaccine programme against malaria has started in Cameroon, in a move projected to save thousands of children's lives across Africa.

The symbolic first jab was given to a baby girl named Daniella at a health facility near Yaoundé on Monday.

Every year 600,000 people die of malaria in Africa, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).

Children under five make up at least 80% of those deaths.

Cameroon is offering the RTS,S vaccine free of charge to all infants up to the age of six months old.

Patients require a total of four doses. Health officials say these will be given at the same time as other routine childhood vaccines to make it easier for parents.

Read fully: https://www.bbc.com/news/world-africa-68037008

*MATERNAL HEALTH AWARENESS DAY*


Maternal Health Awareness Day is celebrated annually on *January 23*, to raise awareness around postpartum health issues and importance of maternal healthcare post childbirth. New mothers are at risk of a range of health complications and mental health issues after giving birth and need support to address these problems. Maternal mortality, though preventable, is still common in many parts of the world.

The Theme for 2024 is Access in Crisis.

Postpartum depression, anxiety, insomnia, increased risk of cardiovascular disease, infections, thyroid issue, urinary incontinence are some of the health problems faced by new mothers. _It is important for the mothers to get continuous care and support from society, communities, government as well as family members._

*Perinatal mood or anxiety disorders* are quite common in women with as many as 1 in 5 women suffering with such disorder during their pregnancy or up to the first 12 months after delivery. Around 80% of them experience symptoms of anxiety, while only 15% are likely to seek help.

*Infection or sepsis of the urinary and uterine tract* are more likely to occur post-delivery and the new mothers may experience pain in their stitches, fever, discharge and burning while urination. Prompt treatment can help in quick recovery.

*Haemorrhage or increased bleeding* can happen in new mothers due to inadequate uterine involution or shrinkage after the baby is delivered. This may happen over 45 days after giving birth.

*Pelvic floor dysfunction* is another health issue that can affect women who have just given birth. The process of pregnancy and giving birth can bring a lot of changes in the pelvic floor and this can lead to urinary incontinence, pelvic pain, and even pain during sex.

The *inflammation of the thyroid gland* can happen after one delivers the baby.

Another major challenge for new mothers is to deal with the *changes in their sleep pattern* considering it could be difficult to adjust to the newborn's sleep-awake cycle.

*DID YOU KNOW?*


The _Anopheles stephensi_ species of mosquito was first detected in Nigeria in *Biliri Local Government Area, Gombe State in 2020* by researchers at Gombe State University working in collaboration with the Nigeria Institute of Medical Research and the National Malaria Elimination Program (NMEP).

In November 2022, PMI (U.S. President’s Malaria Initiative) trained seven researchers, including *Dr. Auwal Al-Hassan*, and 14 entomology technicians selected from universities and research institutes across seven states in the country to strengthen their expertise in surveillance and identification of _An. stephensi_

Dr. Auwal Al-Hassan is a Professor and Entomologist at Abubakar Tafawa Balewa University in Bauchi State, Nigeria. As well as teaching students, he studies insects that transmit diseases and how to control them from spreading.

In Africa, PMI has trained almost 100 researchers and entomologists and 100 community mosquito collectors and insectary technicians on how to monitor _Anopheles stephensi_ behavior and support larval source management to control the mosquitoes and limit the spread of malaria.

From 2017 to 2023, the _PMI VectorLink Project_ has worked across 25 countries in sub-Saharan Africa as well as Cambodia and Colombia to equip countries to plan and implement safe, cost-effective, and sustainable indoor residual spraying, insecticide-treated net distributions, and other life saving interventions to prevent malaria. _PMI VectorLink_ has also strengthened the capacity of country governments to use data to support the optimal deployment of vector control tools within their country.

[24/01/2024, 15:00:35] Pharm Dr . Esty: It is salary week, let us learn our basic labour rights as employees together:

1. You cannot be sacked by your employer after you have submitted your resignation letter. 

2. You cannot submit a resignation letter after you have been sacked.

3. Your employer cannot refuse to accept your letter of resignation. 

Authority: Unity Bank of Nigeria v Bako N. Chori (2021) LPELR-55720 (CA).

4. Your employer cannot deduct your salary as a punishment for something you did wrong at work (e.g. lateness) except if your contract of employment permits this. Otherwise, it is illegal. 

5. Your employer is bound to pay your complete salary when it is due. He is not doing you a favour by paying your salary. You are not expected to beg or request for the salary before it is paid. 

6. If your employer suspends you, you are entitled to receive your full salary for the entire suspension period except where the suspension letter or employee handbook expressly states that you won't receive salary while on suspension. 

Authority: Globe Motors Holdings (Nig) Ltd v Oyewole (2022) LPELR-56856(CA).

*⚕️PHARMACEUTICAL SOCIETY OF NIGERIA*
*YOUNG PHARMACISTS GROUP*
*EDO STATE CHAPTER*

*MEDIA/PUBLICITY/EDITORIAL COMMITTEE*
▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬


It's *CERVICAL CANCER Awareness Month*! Over the past couple of months, there have been emphasis on Cervical Cancer and the HPV Vaccination.


*Globally*, Cervical Cancer is the 4th most common cancer in women. In 2020, there were 604,000 new cases and 342,000 deaths. It is the 4th leading cause of death globally. It is the most commonly diagnosed cancer in about 23 countries and the leading cause of death in about 36 countries. Global inequality in access to healthcare has resulted to high prevalence, incidence and mortality rate.

In *NIGERIA*, Cervical Cancer is the most common genital cancer. In Northern Nigeria, it is the commonest  cancer in women, while in the South, it is second to breast cancer. It is a significant cause of death in women aged 45–65 years in Nigeria. It is yet to be recognized as a public health problem in Nigeria. Women with the cancer in Nigeria, die a painful, miserable and undignified death.

Still in *Nigeria*, approximately 12,075 new cervical cancer cases are diagnosed annually (estimations as at 2020). It is the second most common female cancer diagnosed in the country. Approximately, 8,000 die yearly. 80% of them present at advanced stages. There are huge and almost unsurmountable challenges  of treatment.

Cervical Cancer is caused by persistent infection with *Human Papilloma Virus (HPV)*. HPV is the most commonly sexually transmitted infection. More than 70% of women get infected during their lifetime. Asia and Africa were found to have the highest prevalence of 46% and 30%, respectively.

HPV *risk factors* include: early age at first sexual intercourse (strong risk factor), multiple sexual partners, contact with high-risk men, other STIs, Chlamydia infection, Trichomonas vaginalis infection, HIV, smoking (strong risk factor). Age is a strong risk factor because the transformation zone of the cervix in the young is exposed and poorly developed. HPV is found to be over 70% prevalent among HIV positive women. Cancer explosion can be attributable to multiple factors such as infection, changing population dynamics, behavioural/lifestyle changes, environment and genetics.

The HPV Viruses are DNA viruses. There are more than 100 genotypes. At least, *13 genotypes* can cause cancer. The genotypes that can infect the genital mucosa are either “high risk” or “low risk”. Examples of the *high risk* genotypes are: 16, 18, 31, 33, 35, 39, 45, 51. The 2 genotypes most associates with Cervical cancer are the *genotype 16 and 18*.


The highest rates of cervical cancer incidence and mortality are in low- and middle-income countries. Global *actions towards elimination of Cervical cancer* include: HPV vaccination of females before age 15 years, HPV screening for women with high-quality test by ages 35 and 45 years, treatment of cervical cancer, preventing millions of cervical cancer cases and death.

Prevention of Cervical cancer include: primary, secondary and tertiary prevention. In primary prevention, behavioral change communication and vaccination is involved. Secondary prevention involves Screening (HPV testing, cytology, visual inspections). Tertiary prevention involves the detection and treatment of early cervical cancer.

As at 2022, about 125 countries have introduced HPV vaccination in their national immunization programme for girls and 47 countries for boys.

The target vaccination groups include the *Routine vaccination* (females 9–14 years of age), the *Catch-up vaccination* (females 14–26 years of age who have not been vaccinated previously or who have not completed the full vaccine series), and the *Older women* over 26 years old (whom should be encouraged to discuss HPV immunization with their HCP, and together decide if immunization is appropriate).

There is a 2022 WHO recommendation stating that *a one-dose HPV vaccine* regimen has comparable efficacy and duration of protection as a multi-dose schedule in girls ages 9–14 years. This makes it easier for countries to overcome logistical and resource challenges and increase vaccination coverage levels. Protection duration can be over 20 years for a one-dose vaccination.

The HPV vaccine is not recommended in pregnancy. Vaccination of people with moderate or severe acute illnesses should be deferred until after the illness improves. Minor illnesses should pose no challenge with vaccination.

As healthcare professionals, we should advocate for HPV screening and vaccination. HPV vaccination programme is ongoing in the country. *Free vaccination* is available at vaccination centers for girls between ages 9–14 years. HCPs should also be well trained on cervical cancer and HPV vaccine.

HCPs can ensure the availability of vaccines (at clinics, health centers, pharmacies), recommend vaccination to the general public, engage in campaigns and awareness for HPV and Cervical cancer during related world health days, organize Outreaches and using Outreach mediums. Every health professional body should be engaged and involve its members.

BELOW IS THE PROCEDURE FOR PAYMENT ON THE NEW PCN PAY PORTAL
	*How to Make General Payment*
a.	Visit https://pay.pcn.gov.ng/
b.	Click on “Make General Payment”
c.	Select the appropriate Payment Category
d.	Select the appropriate Payment Type. (The amount to be paid will automatically display; however, in cases where the amount does not automatically display, please get in touch with the PCN office for clarification.)
e.	Enter the appropriate Payment Description
f.	Select the appropriate State Location
g.	Select Payer’s Name, Phone, and Email
h.	Click on “Pay Now.”
i.	Select “Online Payment” as the preferred payment method.
j.	Click on the “Remita” icon
k.	At this point, you can make payment online using your ATM Card via the “Card Option” or obtain the RRR Code to take to the bank via the “Bank Branch” option.

Few days ago, two of Nigeria's online markets, Jumia and Konga, have delisted *Crusader medicated soap*, a cancer-causing cosmetic product, on their platforms. This came after FIJ reported that the two stores and some others were still selling the product. Creamsng, another online store have also delisted the product.

Crusader soap was found to contain *mercury*, which has been found to cause cancer-related terminal illnesses. There is a global action against products, including body creams, containing mercury.

*In September 2023*, NAFDAC arrested a syndicate that specialises in importing banned crusader soaps containing mercury into the country. Prof. Mojisola Adeyeye, NAFDAC's DG, disclosed that the syndicate used forged customs documents to import the product into the country. The importation of the soap into the country was banned by NAFDAC years ago because it contains mercury.

The banned crusader soap was imported 7 times in 2021 alone, by the syndicate. Each consignment is not less than three containers with 4,500 cartons of the soap. The products have found their way into various supermarkets and cosmetic shops with unsuspecting members of the public patronising them.

Adeyeye noted that not one bar of the soap had been manufactured in Nigeria since the purported registration in 2013. Also, claims of the soap been made in England was discovered to be false.

*DID YOU KNOW?*


Recently, one of us came in contact with a parent whose child was born with Glaucoma. Sounds surprising to some of us, right? The good part is that it was detected early, and management started very early. The parent reports that the child is doing well and improving everyday.


*Infantile Glaucoma (Congenital, Paediatric Glaucoma)* occurs in babies and young children. It is usually diagnosed within the first year of life. It is a rare condition that may be inherited, caused by incorrect development of the eye’s drainage system before birth. It leads to increased intraocular pressure, which in turn damages the optic nerve. The symptoms include: enlarged eyes and corner, cloudiness of the cornea, epiphora, photosensitivity, vision loss. Sometimes, no symptoms in some children.

A cloudy cornea is the earliest and most common sign of childhood glaucoma. The healthy cornea is transparent. The loss of this transparency is caused by edema, or swelling of tissue from excess fluid. This occurs in the corneal epithelium (outermost layer) and in the corneal stroma (middle layer) of the cornea tissue. Careful inspection of the cornea may also reveal defects in its inner layer, which is further proof of a raised eye pressure (IOP).

In an uncomplicated case, surgery can often correct the structural defects. Both medication and surgery are required in some cases. Medical treatments may involve the use of topical eye drops and oral medications. These treatments help to either increase the exit of fluid from the eye or decrease the production of fluid inside the eye. Each results in lower eye pressure.

Thousands of children with glaucoma can live full lives. This is the ultimate goal of glaucoma management. Although lost vision cannot be restored, it is possible to optimize each child’s remaining vision. Equally important is to encourage your child’s independence and participation in his or her own self-care.


_Have you encountered this before? Share your thoughts.._

‎[03/02/2024, 09:33:22] Sir Hope Onyemaechi: *VALEDICTORY MESSAGE👋🏻*


Dear Respected YPs,

As I pen down this farewell message, emotions swell within me, reflecting on the extraordinary journey we embarked upon together. From November 1, 2022, to November 1, 2023, and an additional three months that extended my service, this chapter has been one of profound growth, shared accomplishments, and the spirit of unity that defines our vibrant community.

▪️ *Tenure Overview:*

It has been an incredible honor serving as your National Public Relations Officer, and witnessing the growth of our collective aspirations. This period was marked by dedication, hard work, and the pursuit of excellence, and I am proud to have been part of it.

*▪️The Emergence of Pharmacist Daniel Akpan:*

The bye-elections that concluded my term ushered in a new chapter with the emergence of Pharm. Daniel Akpan. As he steps into this role, I extend my heartfelt best wishes for his success. May his tenure be filled with achievements that elevate our group to new heights.


Together, let's now take a moment to reflect on *OUR JOURNEY SO FAR* as well as highlighting some of the notable achievements & laudable exploits recorded over these past fifteen (15) months of my service.

▪️ *Information Flow Mastery:*

Ensuring a seamless and efficient flow of information from the National Body to our dynamic community of Young Pharmacists was a top priority during my tenure. Prompt, timely, and accurate updates were not just a responsibility but a commitment to keeping you informed and empowered

▪️ *Regular Publicity of Job Employment Opportunities for Young Pharmacists*

A cornerstone of our mission has been the consistent and strategic dissemination of job employment opportunities to our dedicated members. The relentless efforts put into this initiative aimed not only at bridging the information gap but also at arming our young pharmacists with the knowledge needed to make informed decisions about their careers. Through regular communication channels and platforms, we endeavored to be a beacon of guidance, ensuring that every aspiring pharmacist had access to promising career paths.

▪️ *Building Quality Relationships:*

One of the most rewarding aspects of my role was establishing quality relationships with as many YPs as possible. In the vast landscape of our community, these connections became the threads that wove a tapestry of unity, collaboration, and shared purpose.

▪️ *Celebrating Excellence:*

Birthdays became more than just calendar milestones; they transformed into opportunities to acknowledge and celebrate outstanding YPs. Recognizing your achievements across various facets of the pharmacy profession added a layer of pride and inspiration to our collective journey.

▪️ *Spearheading the Limelight:*

Under my adept leadership, I orchestrated the colossal publicity for the 4th Annual PSN-YPG Conference at TreasureBase'23, PH, Rivers State, and the resplendent 96th Annual PSN Conference in Jewel City'23, Gombe. My indomitable spirit ensured these events left an indelible mark on the canvas of professional excellence.

▪️ *Accessibility and Prompt Issues Resolution:*

Being at your service around the clock was not just a commitment but a philosophy. Your complaints, challenges, and concerns were met with immediate attention, ensuring a supportive environment for every YP. Together, we navigated the complexities, emerging stronger and more resilient.

▪️ *Empowering Young Minds:*

My commitment to the growth of young pharmacists was exemplified through the massive promotion of capacity-building programs. The Kay-PI (Keeping Pharmacists Informed) initiatives 1.0, 2.0 & 3.0 stand as monumental pillars, fostering knowledge and camaraderie among the aspiring minds in the field.

▪️ *Advocating and Negotiating Competitive Remuneration Packages:*

In our pursuit of excellence, we were not content with merely sharing employment opportunities. We took up the mantle of advocating and negotiating for robust remuneration packages for our members. Recognizing the invaluable contributions young pharmacists make to the healthcare sector, we engaged with employers, ensuring that the financial rewards reflected the dedication and expertise of our members. This advocacy was not just about monetary gains but a commitment to establishing equitable compensation standards within the industry.

▪️ *Ensuring Successful Job Placements:*

Our responsibilities didn't end with advocacy and negotiation. We took proactive steps to follow up on the outcomes, ensuring that the interested individuals didn't just secure job opportunities but embarked on fulfilling and rewarding career journeys. The success stories emerging from these endeavors are a testament to the impact of our collective dedication to the professional growth of young pharmacists.

▪️ *Facilitating Job Opportunities in the South-South Region:*

Our collaboration with AHA was a catalyst for change, resulting in the creation of numerous job opportunities uniquely tailored for young pharmacists in the dynamic South-South Region. By synergizing the resources and networks of both organizations, we succeeded in bridging the gap between aspiring pharmacists and flourishing career paths in this region, leaving an indelible mark on the professional landscape.

▪️ *Instagram Triumph:*

A significant triumph during my tenure was the boost in our YPG Instagram followers. We transformed our online presence, growing from 1620 to an impressive 3,305 followers. This accomplishment not only widened our reach but also strengthened our digital footprint, fostering greater engagement and interaction.

▪️ *Diversification through Innovation:*

I pioneered diversification with avant-garde initiatives like regular sports updates, catering to the sports aficionados within our ranks. Additionally, my updates on various lifestyle trends, both within and outside the profession, added a dynamic facet to our community.

▪️ *Reflecting on Connectivity and Engagement:*

Throughout my tenure, one of the key initiatives was the consolidation of various WhatsApp platforms into two, fostering vibrant engagement and promoting healthy conversations among Young Pharmacists (YPs) nationwide. Additionally, the creation of the Fantasy Premier League (FPL) Platform aimed to infuse the spirit of healthy competition, banter, and excitement associated with the English Premier League (EPL) matches, fostering camaraderie among football enthusiasts.

▪️ *A Collaboration that Redefined Opportunities:*

Undoubtedly, one of the most pivotal moments during my tenure was the strategic partnership forged with Advantage Health Africa (AHA). This collaboration wasn't just a symbolic gesture; it was a transformative alliance that unlocked unparalleled opportunities for young pharmacists, particularly in the South-South Region comprising Edo, Delta, and Rivers.

▪️ *Empowering Young Minds through Certification:*

Collaborating with the National Vice Chairman, I actively participated in promoting and facilitating the certificate training of a total of 152 YPs on three University of Washington certification courses. This initiative not only empowered young minds but also underscored our commitment to continuous learning and professional development.

▪️ *Electoral Committee Leadership:*

Serving as the Ogun PSN-YPG Electoral Committee Chairman in 2023 was a profound experience. Successfully conducting the first official election in the Chapter, we witnessed a formidable set of YPs taking up leadership roles. This marked a crucial step in the continued growth and development of our organization at the grassroots level.

*Information Flow and Public Relations:*

Maintaining a formidable information bridge was paramount, achieved by establishing a platform that housed all PSN-YPG Public Relations Officers across the 37 State Chapters. This strategic move ensured efficient communication and coordination, contributing to the cohesive functioning of the organization.

▪️ *Facilitating State Access and Technical Collaboration:*

A significant achievement was the creation of robust links and avenues granting YPs access to all State PSN-YPG Platforms and various technical groups across the States. This initiative aimed to enhance collaboration, knowledge sharing, and professional development among young pharmacists.

▪️ *Streamlining Dues and Registration Processes:*

In an effort to simplify administrative processes, I took the initiative to create a comprehensive guide for easy step-by-step payment of PCN-related dues, especially via remitta platforms, and provided guidance on various registration processes. This streamlined approach aimed to make bureaucratic tasks more accessible for our members.

▪️ *Scholarship Grant and Honoring a Colleague:*

Actively collaborating with the National Secretariat, we promoted the maiden edition of the Late Princewill Okitche Scholarship Grant for younger PSN-YPG members. This initiative aimed to showcase the creativity of our younger members while immortalizing our beloved friend and colleague, Princewill Okitche, who left us in 2022 while serving as the National Secretary.

In closing, as I pass the baton to Pharm. Daniel Akpan, I express my deepest gratitude for the trust you placed in me. Serving as your National Public Relations Officer has been a privilege and a source of immense pride. I believe in the continued success and prosperity of the PSN-Young Pharmacists Group, and I look forward to witnessing the remarkable achievements that lie ahead.


Thank you for being an integral part of this unforgettable journey. May the spirit of unity and collaboration continue to guide our path. 🙏

Warm regards,

*Pharm. Hope Onyemaechi✍🏽*
*Immediate Past National Public Relations Officer*
*Chairman, National Media/Publicity Team '24*
*PSN-Young Pharmacists Group, Nigeria* ‎image omitted

*WORLD CANCER DAY*


On the 4th of February every year, the world unites to raise awareness on fundamental cancer issues.

The cancer situation in Africa is disheartening. In the year 2020, approximately 1.1 million new cancer cases occurred on the continent, with around 700 000 deaths. About 50% of new cancer cases in adults in Africa are due to breast, cervical, prostate, colorectal, and liver cancers. If urgent measures are not taken, cancer mortality in the region is projected to reach about one million deaths per year by 2030. Also, in 20 years, cancer death rates in Africa will overtake the global average of 30%. This is more so because cancer survival rates in the WHO African region currently average 12%, much lower than the average of over 80% in High-Income Countries. 

Nevertheless, we commend the progress made in cancer prevention and care in our region. For instance, 17 countries have introduced high-performance-based screening tests in line with the WHO recommendations. Also, 28 of our Member States have introduced nationwide HPV vaccination to reach about 60% of the priority population targeted with HPV vaccination.

This year’s theme is auspicious as it reinforces all persons and groups’ universal right to health.  We believe that regardless of socioeconomic status, geographic location, age, and gender, every person must be afforded an equal chance at the prevention, diagnosis, and treatment of cancer. 

We call on the region’s countries, communities, partners, and civil society to unite and foster universal access to cancer prevention and care. 

Stakeholders must identify feasible priorities, implement evidence-based population-wide interventions and invest in cancer control. 

Countries should use the updated WHO Best Buys, the facilitative tool designed to enable governments to select lifesaving policies and interventions for noncommunicable diseases. 

Leaders are responsible for ensuring that cancer prevention and care deploy technologies and therapies that are available at low cost to affected persons and their families, which are value for money. Furthermore, countries should strengthen information systems to gather quality data for decision-making. 

We reiterate that civil society, especially organizations of cancer survivors or persons with lived cancer experiences, are critical in the fight against cancer in Africa. Such a whole-of-society approach to cancer prevention and care is the essence of this year’s World Cancer Day theme.  

“Together, we challenge those in power” to go the extra mile for a cancer-free Africa!

Source: WHO


*Cancer Prevention*

1) Screening tests. Regular screening for early detection of breast, cervical, colorectal cancers, etcetera.

2) Vaccination. Vaccines such as HPV vaccine, Hepatitis B vaccine, etcetera.

3) Healthy choices, such as keeping a healthy weight, avoiding tobacco/smoking, limiting alcohol consumption, regular exercise, healthy diet (poor nutrition contributes), protecting one's skin from excessive sun exposure and cancer causing topical agents.

• Risk factors and cancer
• Foods that protect against cancer
• Foods that may increase cancer risk


*Risk factors and cancer*


Risk factors for Cancer according to CDC include:

1) Alcohol raises one's risk for 6 types of cancer. All alcoholic drinks are linked with cancer.

2) Family health history may increase chance of cancer.

3) Being overweight or having obesity are linked with a higher risk of about 13 types of cancer.

4) Tobacco use and smoking can cause cancer almost anywhere in the body. Quitting is the best. Also, avoiding second-hand smoke.

5) Low fruit and vegetable intake could encourage cancer, as these contain antioxidants that helps combat unhealthy cells. High-fat, low-fibre diets may increase the risk of many cancers including bowel, lung, prostate and uterine cancers.

6) Lack of physical activity or exercise.


A report states that the *strongest protective anti-cancer effect* has been shown with:

1) vegetables, especially raw vegetables or salads, such as leafy green vegetables and carrots

2) foods high in dietary fibre, such as grains and cereals

3) tomatoes, which contains lycopene that is good against prostrate cancer

4) citrus fruits (such as oranges, grapefruit, lemons, limes)

5) cruciferous vegetables like broccoli, cabbage, Brussels sprouts, bok choy and other Asian greens.

More of these vegetables and fruits can be included in one's diet, along with other varieties.


*Foods that may increase cancer risk* include:

1) artificial sweeteners such as aspartame, saccharin and cyclamate. Laboratory rats can develop bladder cancer if fed huge amounts of saccharin or cyclamate, although this is at levels thousands of times greater than a normal diet. International studies have shown that humans are not affected in the same way. Artificial sweeteners are considered safe to eat.

2) cured, pickled or salty foods – bacon and other cured or pickled meats contain a substance called nitrate, which has the potential to cause cancer, and in particular bowel cancer, when eaten in large doses. To be on the safe side, it is best to limit the amount of cured meats in the diet, because they are also generally high in fat and salt. Salt has also been associated with an increased risk of stomach cancer and should be consumed in limited amounts.

3) burnt or barbecued foods – a group of carcinogenic substances called polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) can be produced if foods are overheated or burnt. Although charred or smoked foods could contain traces of PAHs, experts agree that the amount in the average Australian diet is too low to be considered a significant cancer risk. However, when cooking, it’s best to use relatively low temperature methods wherever possible and limit your intake of char-grilled meats and foods. Low-temperature cooking methods include steaming, boiling, poaching, stewing, casseroling, braising, baking, microwaving and roasting.

4) peanuts – some laboratory animals can develop cancer after eating peanuts that are contaminated with toxin-producing moulds.

5) alcohol – consuming alcohol increases the risk of cancers of the mouth, pharynx, larynx, oesophagus, breast, bowel and liver. The risk is even greater in people who smoke. Even small amounts of alcohol can increase your risk. To reduce their risk of disease, men should drink less than 2 standard drinks a day and women less than one standard drink a day.
