[20/02/2026, 07:33:01] ~ Mfon: *The Pharmacist Who Sold His Birthright* 

Chinedu was a brilliant pharmacist.
In the hospital, doctors trusted him.
Patients respected him.
He could detect drug interactions faster than most clinicians.
He was excellent in pharmaceutical care.
But there was one thing he never studied:
Business and professional worth.
One afternoon, a businessman walked into his office.
“Pharmacist, I want to open a wholesale outlet,” the man said confidently.
“I have ₦30 million ready. I just need you to stand as Director for registration. You won’t stress yourself. I will run everything. I will give you ₦2 million once.”
Chinedu paused.
Two million naira.
Instant money.
No capital needed.
No risk — or so he thought.
He replied quietly,
“Okay, I will help.”
And with that simple sentence, he signed the papers.
He became the Pharmacist Director.
On paper.
But not in power.
Not in control.
Not in ownership.
Months passed.
The business grew.
Cartons of drugs came in.
Supplies moved in bulk.
Money flowed.
Yet, Chinedu was never consulted on:
Procurement decisions
Storage conditions
Supplier verification
Compliance documentation
Whenever he asked questions, the investor would say:
“Don’t worry, you are just our director for registration.”
He received his ₦2 million once.
And silence afterwards.
One evening, during a routine inspection, regulators arrived.
They asked one question:
“Who is the Pharmacist Director in charge of this premises?”
The staff pointed to the name on the wall.
Chinedu.
Not the investor.
Not the manager.
Not the accountant.
Chinedu.
Because in law and regulation, the name on record carries the responsibility.
That night, he sat alone and remembered a story he heard as a child.
The story of Esau.
Esau was hungry.
Very hungry.
And in that moment of urgency, he exchanged his birthright for a single meal.
Not because he was foolish.
But because he did not understand the value of what he owned.
Chinedu suddenly whispered to himself:
“I did the same.”
He did not sell land.
He did not sell shares.
He sold something far greater:
His professional birthright — his license, his authority, his regulatory power — for a one-time payment.
Why Did He Take the Esau Route?
It was not greed.
It was lack of orientation.
Like many pharmacists, Chinedu was trained extensively in:
Pharmacology
Therapeutics
Patient care
Clinical interventions
But no one taught him:
Corporate governance
Shareholding structure
Director liability
Professional equity valuation
He knew how drugs interact.
But he did not know how ownership interacts with control.
One day, a senior colleague visited him and asked:
“Chinedu, do you know how the companies you use daily are structured?”
He looked confused.
The senior pharmacist continued,
“Think about the search engine you use for research every day — Google.”
It was founded by Larry Page and Sergey Brin.
They brought innovation.
Investors later brought money.
But did they surrender control?
No.
They used smart share structures — different classes of shares with stronger voting rights — so they could retain decision-making power even when ownership diluted.
They understood something many professionals do not:
Control is more important than cash when responsibility is involved.
The senior pharmacist leaned forward and asked,
“Tell me, Chinedu… if something goes wrong in that warehouse, who will regulators call?”
Chinedu replied slowly,
“My name is on the license…”
“And how much will the investor lose if your license is suspended?”
Silence filled the room.
That was when the truth dawned on him.
He was not paid ₦2 million for a role.
He was paid ₦2 million for risk transfer.
The investor had transferred:
Legal risk
Regulatory accountability
Professional liability
To the pharmacist who had the least control.


 *The Real Lesson* 
Most pharmacists are excellent in pharmaceutical care.
But very few study:
Business structures
Share interpretation
Professional valuation
Governance rights
So when an offer comes, they evaluate it like a salary, instead of evaluating it like a director-level responsibility.
They ask:
“How much am I being paid?”
Instead of asking:
“What am I legally responsible for?”
Years later, Chinedu began teaching young pharmacists.
He would tell them:
“Your license is not a rubber stamp.
It is a regulatory asset.
It is professional equity.
It is your birthright.”
Then he would add quietly,
“Esau sold his birthright because he was hungry.
Many pharmacists do the same — not for food, but for quick money and lack of orientation.”

The Professional Reflection: 

 *Knowing the Worth of Your Birthright* 
Think for a moment.
When a lawyer prepares a deed of agreement, what does he earn?
A percentage of the transaction value.
When a real estate agent connects a buyer to a house, what does he earn?
Often 5–10% of the value of the property.
Why?
Because they provide access, structure, and legal legitimacy.
Now ask yourself as a pharmacist:
What is the value of:
Your license?
Your regulatory access?
Your professional accountability?
Your legal responsibility before regulators?
These are high-risk professional assets.
Yet many pharmacists accept a one-off payment that is less than what a consultant or agent would earn in a single transaction — while carrying lifelong regulatory liability.
License is Not Just a Name — It is Regulatory Capital
Without a pharmacist:
The premises cannot be properly registered
Regulatory compliance cannot stand
Professional oversight cannot be validated
Your license is not a mere formality.
It is regulatory infrastructure.
And regulatory infrastructure has value.
The Figurehead Trap
When a pharmacist collects a small one-off fee and becomes a “director on paper,” they transfer:
Legal exposure
Professional reputation
Regulatory liability
In exchange for short-term compensation.
This is risk outsourcing disguised as opportunity.

A *Better Way to Think (Professional Valuation Mindset)* 

Instead of saying:
“I am not bringing money.”
A professionally oriented pharmacist should think:
“I am bringing license value, regulatory legitimacy, and governance accountability.”
Discussions should start with:
Equity structure
Governance control
Retainership or professional compensation
Clearly defined legal responsibility


 *The Final Advisory to Pharmacists* 
Do not reduce your professional worth to a token payment.
Do not exchange long-term liability for short-term comfort.
Do not become a figurehead in a structure where you bear responsibility without control.
Because in regulated professions, the name on record is accountable — not ceremonial.
Before signing any document, pause and ask:
Am I a partner or a placeholder?
Do I have control or just a title?
Am I being compensated for my risk or silenced with a one-off payment?
Your license is not a rubber stamp.
It is not a signature for hire.
It is your professional birthright.
And no pharmacist should trade a lifelong regulatory identity for a meagre one-off fee and become a figurehead in a system where responsibility is real, but power is absent

Written by 
Pharm Avwenaghagha Ochuko.

TRIBUTE TO PROF. CYRIL ODIANOSE USIFOH AT 65
A Life of Conviction, Courage, and Professional Statesmanship

Today, we celebrate a remarkable milestone in the life of an extraordinary pharmacist, scholar, and statesman — Prof Cyril Usifoh — as he turns 65.

Sixty-five years is not merely a passage of time; it is a testimony of impact. It is a ledger of service rendered, battles fought, standards defended, and generations inspired.

A Scholar with Depth and Discipline

Prof. Usifoh’s intellectual journey reflects discipline, scholarship, and an unwavering commitment to pharmaceutical excellence. As an academic, he has shaped minds not only with knowledge but with values — insisting that competence must walk hand in hand with character.

In lecture halls and professional forums alike, he has demonstrated that pharmacy is not merely a profession; it is a public trust.

A Courageous Professional Leader

As former President of the Pharmaceutical Society of Nigeria and current Chairman of Membership Committee of the Nigeria Academy of Pharmacy, Prof. Usifoh provided leadership at a time when clarity, firmness, and advocacy were required.

Leadership, especially in professional associations, demands more than popularity. It requires courage — the courage to defend standards, to speak truth to power, and to insist on regulatory integrity even when the path is uncomfortable.

Prof. Usifoh has shown that professional leadership is a form of stewardship. And stewardship demands accountability to both members and the public.

A Defender of Professional Integrity

In a rapidly evolving healthcare landscape — with regulatory pressures, distribution reforms, and systemic restructuring — voices of clarity are rare and precious. Prof. Usifoh has been one of those voices.

He has consistently championed:
	•	Professional autonomy
	•	Ethical pharmacy practice
	•	Regulatory strengthening
	•	The protection of standards
	•	The dignity of pharmacists within the healthcare ecosystem

Such advocacy is not always convenient. But it is always necessary.

A Mentor to the Next Generation

At 65, the most enduring measure of impact is not titles held, but people raised.

Across institutions, professional bodies, and leadership platforms, Prof. Usifoh has invested in younger pharmacists — encouraging boldness, competence, and principled engagement.

The profession moves forward because men like him refused to compromise its foundations.

The Significance of 65

In many cultures, 65 represents maturity crowned with wisdom. It is an age where experience speaks with authority, and reflection deepens insight.

Yet, for leaders of Prof. Usifoh’s calibre, 65 is not retirement from relevance — it is refinement of influence.

The season ahead is not smaller. It is wider.

It is a season for:
	•	Advisory wisdom
	•	Institutional strengthening
	•	Intergenerational mentorship
	•	Strategic reform
	•	Legacy building

A Personal Note of Respect

As colleagues in advancing pharmacy and institutional reform, we recognise that authentic leadership is tested in seasons of tension. It is proven when principles are non-negotiable.

Prof. Cyril Usifoh has shown that the profession must never be casual about its destiny.

History remembers not those who drifted with the tide, but those who steadied the ship.

Birthday Wishes

On this landmark 65th birthday, we celebrate:
	•	Your scholarship
	•	Your conviction
	•	Your service
	•	Your courage
	•	Your contribution to Nigerian pharmacy

May this new chapter bring you:
	•	Renewed strength
	•	Expanded influence
	•	Divine health
	•	Enduring relevance
	•	And the deep satisfaction that comes from knowing you stood firm where it mattered most

Happy 65th Birthday, Prof. Cyril Odianose Usifoh.

Your impact is written not only in policy documents and professional resolutions, but in the lives and standards you have helped shape.

And that legacy endures.

PLB

[20/02/2026, 10:47:00] St. Pharm  Yp Justine: *How to carry out premises registration for the year*

Determine the nature of the premise if it's wholesale or retail

Go on https://pay.pcn.gov.ng and pay the amount that pertains to the nature of your premise. Wholesale is 150k..  retail is 10k

Print the receipt of payment 

Go on https://pharmagateway.com.ng and pay the relevant dues which must include the Acpn dues in this case.

Download the soft copy of the receipt 

Go to https://www.psnedo.com upload the receipt and request for clearance. 

Once cleared print the clearance slip 

Go to https://acpnedo.macrosxp.com upload the receipt and request for clearance 

Once cleared print the clearance slip

Gather all the printouts with your application for renewal and go to the council for registration.

[21/02/2026, 08:10:04] Gwerkky Ypgd: *The Pharmacist Who Sold His Birthright* 

Chinedu was a brilliant pharmacist.
In the hospital, doctors trusted him.
Patients respected him.
He could detect drug interactions faster than most clinicians.
He was excellent in pharmaceutical care.
But there was one thing he never studied:
Business and professional worth.
One afternoon, a businessman walked into his office.
“Pharmacist, I want to open a wholesale outlet,” the man said confidently.
“I have ₦30 million ready. I just need you to stand as Director for registration. You won’t stress yourself. I will run everything. I will give you ₦2 million once.”
Chinedu paused.
Two million naira.
Instant money.
No capital needed.
No risk — or so he thought.
He replied quietly,
“Okay, I will help.”
And with that simple sentence, he signed the papers.
He became the Pharmacist Director.
On paper.
But not in power.
Not in control.
Not in ownership.
Months passed.
The business grew.
Cartons of drugs came in.
Supplies moved in bulk.
Money flowed.
Yet, Chinedu was never consulted on:
Procurement decisions
Storage conditions
Supplier verification
Compliance documentation
Whenever he asked questions, the investor would say:
“Don’t worry, you are just our director for registration.”
He received his ₦2 million once.
And silence afterwards.
One evening, during a routine inspection, regulators arrived.
They asked one question:
“Who is the Pharmacist Director in charge of this premises?”
The staff pointed to the name on the wall.
Chinedu.
Not the investor.
Not the manager.
Not the accountant.
Chinedu.
Because in law and regulation, the name on record carries the responsibility.
That night, he sat alone and remembered a story he heard as a child.
The story of Esau.
Esau was hungry.
Very hungry.
And in that moment of urgency, he exchanged his birthright for a single meal.
Not because he was foolish.
But because he did not understand the value of what he owned.
Chinedu suddenly whispered to himself:
“I did the same.”
He did not sell land.
He did not sell shares.
He sold something far greater:
His professional birthright — his license, his authority, his regulatory power — for a one-time payment.
Why Did He Take the Esau Route?
It was not greed.
It was lack of orientation.
Like many pharmacists, Chinedu was trained extensively in:
Pharmacology
Therapeutics
Patient care
Clinical interventions
But no one taught him:
Corporate governance
Shareholding structure
Director liability
Professional equity valuation
He knew how drugs interact.
But he did not know how ownership interacts with control.
One day, a senior colleague visited him and asked:
“Chinedu, do you know how the companies you use daily are structured?”
He looked confused.
The senior pharmacist continued,
“Think about the search engine you use for research every day — Google.”
It was founded by Larry Page and Sergey Brin.
They brought innovation.
Investors later brought money.
But did they surrender control?
No.
They used smart share structures — different classes of shares with stronger voting rights — so they could retain decision-making power even when ownership diluted.
They understood something many professionals do not:
Control is more important than cash when responsibility is involved.
The senior pharmacist leaned forward and asked,
“Tell me, Chinedu… if something goes wrong in that warehouse, who will regulators call?”
Chinedu replied slowly,
“My name is on the license…”
“And how much will the investor lose if your license is suspended?”
Silence filled the room.
That was when the truth dawned on him.
He was not paid ₦2 million for a role.
He was paid ₦2 million for risk transfer.
The investor had transferred:
Legal risk
Regulatory accountability
Professional liability
To the pharmacist who had the least control.


 *The Real Lesson* 
Most pharmacists are excellent in pharmaceutical care.
But very few study:
Business structures
Share interpretation
Professional valuation
Governance rights
So when an offer comes, they evaluate it like a salary, instead of evaluating it like a director-level responsibility.
They ask:
“How much am I being paid?”
Instead of asking:
“What am I legally responsible for?”
Years later, Chinedu began teaching young pharmacists.
He would tell them:
“Your license is not a rubber stamp.
It is a regulatory asset.
It is professional equity.
It is your birthright.”
Then he would add quietly,
“Esau sold his birthright because he was hungry.
Many pharmacists do the same — not for food, but for quick money and lack of orientation.”

The Professional Reflection: 

 *Knowing the Worth of Your Birthright* 
Think for a moment.
When a lawyer prepares a deed of agreement, what does he earn?
A percentage of the transaction value.
When a real estate agent connects a buyer to a house, what does he earn?
Often 5–10% of the value of the property.
Why?
Because they provide access, structure, and legal legitimacy.
Now ask yourself as a pharmacist:
What is the value of:
Your license?
Your regulatory access?
Your professional accountability?
Your legal responsibility before regulators?
These are high-risk professional assets.
Yet many pharmacists accept a one-off payment that is less than what a consultant or agent would earn in a single transaction — while carrying lifelong regulatory liability.
License is Not Just a Name — It is Regulatory Capital
Without a pharmacist:
The premises cannot be properly registered
Regulatory compliance cannot stand
Professional oversight cannot be validated
Your license is not a mere formality.
It is regulatory infrastructure.
And regulatory infrastructure has value.
The Figurehead Trap
When a pharmacist collects a small one-off fee and becomes a “director on paper,” they transfer:
Legal exposure
Professional reputation
Regulatory liability
In exchange for short-term compensation.
This is risk outsourcing disguised as opportunity.

A *Better Way to Think (Professional Valuation Mindset)* 

Instead of saying:
“I am not bringing money.”
A professionally oriented pharmacist should think:
“I am bringing license value, regulatory legitimacy, and governance accountability.”
Discussions should start with:
Equity structure
Governance control
Retainership or professional compensation
Clearly defined legal responsibility


 *The Final Advisory to Pharmacists* 
Do not reduce your professional worth to a token payment.
Do not exchange long-term liability for short-term comfort.
Do not become a figurehead in a structure where you bear responsibility without control.
Because in regulated professions, the name on record is accountable — not ceremonial.
Before signing any document, pause and ask:
Am I a partner or a placeholder?
Do I have control or just a title?
Am I being compensated for my risk or silenced with a one-off payment?
Your license is not a rubber stamp.
It is not a signature for hire.
It is your professional birthright.
And no pharmacist should trade a lifelong regulatory identity for a meagre one-off fee and become a figurehead in a system where responsibility is real, but power is absent

Written by 
Pharm Avwenaghagha Ochuko.

The Management of the University of Benin Teaching Hospital (UBTH) has noted with grave concern the circulation of false, misleading, and malicious publications targeted at the Chief Medical Director (CMD) of the Hospital, Prof (Mrs) Idia Nibokun Ize-Iyamu, in some sections of social media, particularly regarding the engagement of a private laboratory service within the Accident and Emergency (A&E) Unit.

Management states unequivocally that these allegations are entirely false, defamatory, and devoid of factual or legal basis, and appear calculated to mislead the public, incite distrust, and unjustly impugn the integrity of the Chief Medical Director and the institution.

For clarity, the private laboratory service was engaged to complement the Hospital’s existing diagnostic services within the A&E Unit. The decision was taken strictly in the overriding interest of patient care and safety, particularly for critically ill patients whose survival depends on immediate and uninterrupted access to laboratory investigations especially when there are challenges with the UBTH laboratory in the Accident and Emergency unit. 

This engagement was neither arbitrary nor unlawful but fully compliant with extant Federal Ministry of Health (FMoH) directives, which empower hospital managements to adopt innovative arrangements to ensure the continuity of critical healthcare services. The service is intended to function alongside the Hospital’s laboratories, augmenting capacity and efficiency, and not to replace or supplant the hospital’s core laboratory services. Indeed, there exist over ten (10) functional hospital laboratories across UBTH and they continue to operate, clearly negating any insinuation of institutional displacement or privatization.

Management therefore rejects in the strongest terms the reckless dissemination of falsehoods and cautions and wish to state that the continued publication or repetition of these defamatory claims may attract appropriate legal action, as UBTH reserves the right to protect the reputation of its leadership and institution through all lawful means.

Members of the public are accordingly advised to disregard these spurious allegations and rely solely on verified information issued through official channels of the University of Benin Teaching Hospital.

UBTH remains steadfast in its statutory mandate to deliver quality healthcare, uphold professional ethics, and safeguard lives, regardless of prevailing challenges.

 _Kidney Health For All — Caring for People, Protecting the Planet_
 
Kidney stones are more than just a painful diagnosis; they are a significant burden on Nigeria's healthcare system. If left unmanaged, complications can lead to chronic kidney disease and the life-altering reality of dialysis.

[13/03/2026, 21:06:31] King Penet: **ANNOUNCEMENT: Important Update on Job Postings – Especially for Superintendent Pharmacists**

Hello everyone,

We want to let you know about a small but important change to how **all job postings**, especially for **Superintendent Pharmacist** roles, are now handled.

In the past, all jobs were sent directly to the JAEC team, who would vet and post them in our WhatsApp groups. Going forward, jobs can either be sent to the JAEC team **or** submitted through our official website — where the JAEC team will review and approve them once they meet the basic requirements.

**Please note:**  
🚫 Direct job posts or advertisements for Superintendent Pharmacist (or any pharmacy role) will no longer be allowed in this WhatsApp group.

### Why this change?
- To make job postings more **organized and reliable**
- To ensure all opportunities are **verified and easy to track**
- To provide a **central, professional platform** for pharmacy jobs
- To reduce group clutter and make it easier for everyone to find what matters
- To encourage more members to use the **PSN YPG EDO website**

### How to post a job on the website:
- ✅ All standard job postings are **FREE for the first 20 days**
- ✅ After 20 days, posts will expire — but can be renewed
- ✅ Want more visibility? You can choose a **featured (paid) advert** — this is optional and helps your post stand out

**To post a job:**
1. Visit **www.psnypgedo.org**
2. Go to the **"Post a Job"** or **"Advertise"** section
3. Fill in the job details (role, requirements, location, salary, etc.)
4. Submit — your post will be reviewed and published shortly

Please share this update with your networks so everyone stays informed. This is a step toward making our community more professional and accessible for all.

If you have any questions or need help with posting, don’t hesitate to reach out.

Thanks for your cooperation and support!

Best regards,  
13th March 2026

[14/03/2026, 08:52:38] ~ Pharm AJ: *How I Became a Regulatory Pharmacist*

A few months ago, I was curious about Regulatory Affairs but didn’t know how to break into the field.

I enrolled in the NAFDAC Drug & Nutraceuticals Registration Training (Cohort 1), and what stood out immediately was how practical the sessions were. We learned how regulatory work actually happens: reviewing CTD documents, understanding NAPAMS applications, and how product registrations move through NAFDAC.

Shortly after the training, I secured a role as a Regulatory Officer with a pharmaceutical company in Lagos. Many of the tasks I now handle at work were things we had already discussed during the training.

The mentorship and support after the training has also been incredibly helpful as I continue to grow in the role.

Today, I’m building a career in Regulatory Affairs, and enrolling in that training was the step that opened the door.

*Pharm. Daniel A., Lagos*

[16/03/2026, 17:26:44] Mayowa Fasiku: *🔊ANNOUNCEMENT*

*📍PSN EDO  CLEARANCE*

1. Kindly make all your dues payment via PSNPAY website (www.psnpay.com.ng), Pharmagateway website (www. Pharmagateway.com.ng) or Pharmpay (download via Google play store).

2. After making your payment download the receipt for subsequent usage.

3. Log on to PSN EDO website *(www.psnedo.com)* *Fill in all necessary information and upload your dues  payment slip from either Pharmagateway or Pharmpay*

4. As a first timer on the website you are expected to Sign up

5. Your subsequent log in details will be;
 *Username: Phone Number*
 *Number Password: PCN Reg number*

6. After registration, you may have to wait for sometime to get your clearance slip on your dashboard. 

*NB. Members are to please follow this process for a seamless registration*

*ACPN members are to ensure they have their ACPN clearance slip before they proceed to the Edo PSN portal*

 The Federal Government has declared Thursday, March 19, and Friday, March 20, 2026, as public holidays to mark the celebration of Eid-el-Fitr, which signifies the end of the Muslim holy month of Ramadan.

The declaration was made by the Minister of Interior, Olubunmi Tunji-Ojo, on behalf of the Federal Government.

In a statement on Tuesday by the Permanent Secretary of the ministry, Magdalene Ajani, the minister extended warm greetings and heartfelt congratulations to Muslim faithful on the successful completion of the fasting period.

Tunji-Ojo urged Muslims to sustain the virtues of love, generosity, peace, tolerance and sacrifice, which were emphasised during the holy month of Ramadan.

He also called on Nigerians to use the festive period to pray for the continued peace, unity and prosperity of the country.

While wishing Muslim faithful a joyful Eid-ul-Fitr celebration, the minister encouraged citizens to celebrate responsibly and extend acts of kindness to the less privileged in society.

He added that the Federal Government remains committed to fostering national unity and peaceful coexistence among all Nigerians.

Even if you drank plenty water at night?

It’s because after 6–8 hours of sleep, your body is already slightly dehydrated.

You haven’t had any fluids all night, but your body kept breathing, sweating, and working.

• Helps wake up your brain
• Improves concentration
• Supports digestion
• Helps bowel movement
• Rehydrates your body

Water first. Coffee later. Your body will thank you.

[25/03/2026, 17:08:16] Pharm Wendy Healrh Centre: *Child hasn't pooped in 3 days?*
Constipation is very common in children, especially when
- Starting solids
- Not drinking enough water
- Taking too much milk
- Eating too much rice, bread, or bananas.

Try this:
• Give more water
• Pawpaw, pear, or prunes
• Tummy massage
• Bicycle legs
• Warm bath

If still hard, doctor or pharmacist may recommend a stool softener.

Go to the hospital if there is vomiting, swollen tummy, blood in stool, or no poo for more than 5 days.

Black-eyed peas — Nigerian English: BEANS | Yoruba: EPA | Igbo: Àgwà

[31/03/2026, 11:56:23] Sir Prof  Pharm Abu Dantani John: *IMPORTANT ANNOUNCEMENT!*

*🛑 STEPWISE PROCESSES TO OBTAIN ACPN CLEARANCE* 🛑

1. Kindly make all your dues payment via Pharmagateway website (www.Pharmagateway.com.ng) or Pharmpay (download via Google play store).

2. After making your payment download the receipt for subsequent use.

3. Log in to EDO ACPN website *(https://www.acpnedo.com/)* *Fill in all necessary information and upload your dues  payment slip from either Pharmagateway or Pharmpay*

4. As a first timer on the website you are expected to Sign up

5. Your subsequent log in details will be;
 *Username: Phone Number*
 *Number Password: Your registered password*

6. DO NOT UPLOAD THE PAYSTACK RECEIPT BUT THE RECEIPT THAT HAS THE DUES BREAKDOWN 

7. After registration, you may have to wait for sometime to get your clearance slip on your dashboard. 


*Please obtain your ACPN clearance before proceeding for PSN clearance*

*Announcer:*
Pharm Abu Dantani John 
(Secretary)

*Signed:*
Dr Nwachukwu Idemili 
(Chairman)

*DOMINION OVER FEAR OF DEATH*

*Friday, April 3rd*

*Pastor Chris*

_*Forasmuch then as the children are partakers of flesh and blood, he also himself likewise took part of the same; that through death he might destroy him that had the power of death, that is, the devil; And deliver them who through fear of death were all their lifetime subject to bondage (Hebrews 2:14-15).*_

The scripture above is as clear as it is emphatic: the Lord Jesus has completely destroyed the one who had the power of death, the devil, and delivered humanity from the fear of death. He didn’t come to give us a partial victory. His work wasn’t unfinished or incomplete. He fully defeated Satan who had the power of death. 

2 Timothy 1:10 says, He _*"…abolished death, and hath brought life and immortality to light through the gospel."*_ He replaced death with life and deathlessness. Hallelujah! This is the message of faith. This is the Word of the Gospel: death has been abolished. 

Consider the early apostles; they didn’t die because they grew old or weak. The Scriptures reveal that their departure from this world was consistent with their specific calling and choice to seal the message of the Gospel with their blood. They laid down their lives; death had no power over them. 

The Christian life is the transcendent life, not a slow succumbing to death, corruption or decay. You were not designed to “wear out.” The life of God in you is incorruptible; it’s divine; it’s ageless. It doesn’t diminish or deteriorate. You’re in the death-free and fear-free zone. Live in Christ’s victory every day: fearless, strong and full of life. Praise God!

*I’m fearless and bold, living in the consciousness that the Lord Jesus has abolished death and brought me into life and immortality. I walk in strength, health and glory. I live in Christ’s victory: fearless, strong and full of life. Amen.*
